summary: Discusses the problem statement and use cases for IPv6 vehicular networking in intelligent transportation systems, including vehicle-to-vehicle, vehicle-to-infrastructure, and vehicle-to-everything communication. It analyzes gaps in existing IPv6 protocols for these environments.

eli5.summary: Cars may talk to each other and to roadside gear. This lists what is needed and where the current internet rules do not fit moving vehicles.

questions: how do connected vehicles use ipv6
subtitle: Communication scenarios and IPv6 requirements for connected and autonomous vehicles.

tldr.problem: Intelligent transportation systems need vehicles to communicate with each other, with roadside infrastructure, and with devices, but today's IPv6 protocols were not designed for the high-speed, short-contact-time environment of vehicle networks where traditional neighbor discovery and handoff procedures are too slow.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9365 catalogs real-world use cases for vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V), vehicle-to-infrastructure (V2I), and vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communications using IPv6. It documents the gaps in existing IPv6 protocols—particularly in Neighbor Discovery, mobility management, security, and privacy—that prevent IPv6 from working well in vehicular environments.
tldr.outcome: This RFC motivates development of IPv6-based protocols and extensions tailored to vehicular networks, establishing a foundation for future work on IPWAVE (IPv6 Wireless Access in Vehicular Environments) and other vehicle networking standards.

facts.label: Dwelling time (example)
facts.value: 72 seconds at 100 km/h in 1 km DSRC range

today: RFC 9365 is an informational specification documenting the problem statement and use cases for IPv6-based vehicular networks. It serves as a foundation for ongoing IETF standardization work on vehicular network protocols. Some vehicular communication systems (DSRC and C-V2X) have been deployed in countries including the US, EU, and Japan, creating real-world demand for IPv6 protocol extensions tailored to vehicular environments.

sections.title: Connected and Autonomous Vehicles
sections.content:
Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS) are systems designed to improve road safety, traffic efficiency, and the driving experience through technology. Today's vehicles face regulations and opportunities from governments worldwide: the FCC in the US allocated the 5.9 GHz band for Dedicated Short-Range Communications (DSRC), the EU allocated radio spectrum in the 5.875 - 5.905 GHz band, and most other countries have adopted similar allocations for vehicular communication.

Physical and data-link standards for these communications already exist. IEEE 802.11p (now part of 802.11-OCB) defines the wireless interface, and 3GPP has standardized Cellular Vehicle-to-Everything (C-V2X) for both LTE and 5G networks. However, the network layer remains an open question. This RFC proposes using IPv6 as the common IP-layer protocol for vehicular networks, enabling vehicles to use IPv6-based mobility protocols like Mobile IPv6, Proxy Mobile IPv6, and Distributed Mobility Management. It outlines what needs to be standardized to make IPv6 work well in vehicular environments.
sections.eli5: Cars worldwide are getting permission and equipment to talk wirelessly. They need an internet protocol for the network layer. IPv6 is a candidate, but it needs adjustments for the unique environment of moving vehicles.

sections.title: Vehicle Communication Scenarios
sections.content:
The RFC defines three main communication scenarios. Vehicle-to-Vehicle (V2V) allows direct wireless communication between vehicles. Use cases include context-aware navigation (alerting drivers to hazards and obstacles in real time), collision avoidance for urban air mobility (drones), cooperative adaptive cruise control (vehicles automatically adjusting speed relative to neighbors), platooning (trucks or buses moving in close formation to reduce fuel consumption), and cooperative environment sensing (vehicles sharing data from radars, LiDAR, and cameras).

Vehicle-to-Infrastructure (V2I) connects vehicles to fixed roadside equipment. Use cases include navigation services coordinated with a Traffic Control Center, energy-efficient speed recommendations based on traffic conditions, accident notification and emergency services, electric vehicle charging coordination, and urban air mobility navigation with efficient battery charging.

Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) extends beyond vehicles to include devices and pedestrians. The primary use case discussed is protection for vulnerable road users (pedestrians and cyclists) equipped with smartphones. A pedestrian's device can communicate with nearby vehicles to alert drivers and reduce collision risk.
sections.eli5: V2V is car-to-car. V2I is car-to-roadside equipment. V2X is car-to-anything-else. Each has different applications: safety, navigation, and pedestrian protection.

sections.title: Vehicular Network Architecture
sections.content:
RFC 9365 defines hardware components for vehicular networks. An IP On-Board Unit (IP-OBU) is a computer in a vehicle with IPv6 connectivity and radio interfaces for wireless communication with other vehicles and roadside units. An IP Roadside Unit (IP-RSU) is a fixed infrastructure node along the road with both wireless interfaces (for communicating with vehicles) and wired interfaces (for connecting to other network infrastructure). A Mobility Anchor (MA) maintains IPv6 address bindings and mobility information for vehicles, similar to a home agent in Mobile IPv6.

Vehicles can form a connected network topology where some vehicles communicate directly with roadside infrastructure (V2I) and others relay through neighboring vehicles when out of range (multihop V2V or V2I2V). The RFC shows example architectures where multiple roadside units manage separate subnets, vehicles move between their coverage areas, and internal networks within vehicles (containing multiple hosts and routers) must interoperate with fixed infrastructure networks and other vehicle networks. Each vehicle or roadside unit is responsible for advertising its own network prefixes and managing its own address space.
sections.eli5: Vehicles have special computers (IP-OBUs) for wireless communication. Roadside boxes (IP-RSUs) handle infrastructure. Mobility anchors track vehicles as they move. Together they form a network where vehicles can talk directly or through relays.

sections.title: IPv6 Protocol Gaps and Requirements
sections.content:
RFC 9365 identifies specific challenges in applying standard IPv6 to vehicular networks. Neighbor Discovery must be extended to work in highly mobile environments where neighbors appear and disappear in seconds. Traditional IPv6 ND assumes relatively stable network links; in vehicular networks, a vehicle at highway speeds passing an IP-RSU has only about 72 seconds of connectivity. The RFC notes that vehicles need efficient address autoconfiguration, rapid detection of new neighbors, and reliable neighbor reachability in a high-loss wireless environment.

Mobility Management must support handovers between subnets with minimal packet loss. When a vehicle moves from one IP-RSU's coverage to another's, its IPv6 address must change, but ongoing TCP sessions and UDP flows should continue with minimal disruption. Traditional Mobile IPv6 designs assume a home network and care-of address, but vehicular networks involve rapid, unpredictable movement among multiple possible anchors.

Security and Privacy must protect vehicles from spoofing attacks, eavesdropping, and tracking. MAC address and IPv6 address pseudonyms can hide vehicle identity, but their frequency of change must balance anonymity with practicality. Authentication between vehicles must happen before they cooperate (e.g., before platooning). The RFC emphasizes that vehicular networks expose more personal data (location, speed, driving patterns) than traditional networks, requiring careful privacy safeguards.
sections.eli5: IPv6 has three main problems in vehicles: neighbor discovery happens too slowly when contacts last seconds, mobility handoffs lose packets during subnet changes, and vehicles need strong privacy since their location data is sensitive.

sections.title: Roadmap and Standards Impact
sections.content:
RFC 9365 is an informational RFC that documents problem statements and use cases rather than specifying complete solutions. It identifies areas requiring further standardization: extensions to IPv6 Neighbor Discovery for vehicular use (called Vehicular ND or VND), extensions to IPv6 mobility management for vehicular networks (called Vehicular Mobility Management or VMM), and security and privacy mechanisms for vehicular networks (called Vehicular Security and Privacy or VSP).

The RFC references ISO standards for CALM (Communications Access for Land Mobiles) that also specify IPv6 for vehicular networks, demonstrating alignment between IETF and ISO initiatives. It also notes that WAVE standards (IEEE 802.11p and related specifications) have already been deployed in some countries, creating pressure to standardize IPv6 at the network layer. The document serves as motivation for future IETF work on IPWAVE (IPv6 Wireless Access in Vehicular Environments) and other protocol extensions needed to make IPv6 practical for connected and autonomous vehicles.
sections.eli5: This RFC lists what needs to be built and standardized. It's a roadmap document that motivated future standards work on IPv6 for vehicles. Real deployments in some countries are already driving this work forward.
